stories.headline: Magnitude 7.7 Earthquake Strikes Indonesia's Flores Region, Tsunami Warning Issued
stories.summary:
A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia's Flores region early Saturday, with the U.S. Geological Survey reporting a shallow depth of 10 kilometers and an epicenter roughly 68 kilometers northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. Several aftershocks followed the initial quake, and Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency issued a tsunami warning covering parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi, and Southeast Sulawesi provinces.

Residents across Flores Island felt strong shaking, with initial reports indicating damage to homes and public facilities. A resident of Sikka described collapsed structures, including a waiting room at the Maumere port terminal, as panicked residents fled to higher ground. Officials had not yet released casualty figures or comprehensive damage estimates as of early reports.

The Flores region has a deadly seismic history — a magnitude 7.0 earthquake there in 1992 triggered a tsunami that killed approximately 2,500 people. Indonesia sits on the 'Ring of Fire' and is among the world's most earthquake-prone nations, with its archipelago of more than 17,000 islands regularly experiencing significant seismic activity. Authorities urged coastal residents to move to higher ground and were monitoring tide gauges for tsunami activity.

stories.headline: Trump Visits New York Police Academy, Touts Record-Low Homicide Rate Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump traveled to the Nassau County police academy on Long Island Friday to promote new FBI crime statistics showing the U.S. homicide rate dropped to its lowest level in 75 years in 2025. The visit was framed as a midterm campaign boost for Republicans contesting competitive New York races, though Trump's approval ratings remain under pressure amid an ongoing and unpopular war with Iran.

While briefly highlighting the crime data, Trump quickly pivoted to partisan attacks, calling opponents 'Radical left Democrats' and 'Dumb-ocrats,' insulting Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, and referring to state Attorney General Letitia James — who successfully sued Trump for financial fraud — as 'a real slob' and 'a disgrace.' He also touted his deployment of the National Guard to U.S. cities and credited his administration with making Washington safer.

Supporters credit the administration's aggressive law enforcement posture with driving the crime decline, while critics argue the downward trend predates Trump's tenure and note that his campaign-style remarks at a uniformed police event blurred the line between governance and electioneering. Democrats have pointed to soaring gasoline prices and the Iran war's economic toll as the more pressing issues for voters heading into November.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He'll 'Never Apologize' for Higher Gas Prices, Calls Iran War a Necessary Trade-Off
stories.summary:
President Trump, speaking in New York Friday, defended record-high August gasoline prices by framing them as an acceptable cost of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. 'I'll never apologize,' Trump said, arguing that Americans should be willing to pay 'a tiny bit more' at the pump in exchange for the military campaign against Tehran.

Democratic Representative Gwen Moore of Wisconsin pushed back sharply, saying even modest fuel price increases were creating 'chaos and hardship' for families already stretched by persistent inflation. Moore and other Democrats have sought to tie the economic squeeze directly to the administration's Iran policy ahead of November's midterm elections.

Republican Representative Mike Flood of Nebraska acknowledged that affordability remains a top constituent concern, though he stopped short of criticizing the president's Iran strategy. The exchange captures the central political fault line heading into the midterms: Republicans arguing the war is a national security imperative, Democrats framing it as an economic burden falling on working families. Gasoline prices have already been reported at their highest level for this time of year on record.

stories.headline: Update: Aid Activists Blocked From Reaching Besieged Palestinian Families in West Bank Village of Qusra
stories.summary:
Activists attempted Friday to deliver food and water to two Palestinian families trapped in their homes in the West Bank village of Qusra, where Israeli settlers have maintained a siege since Sunday, cutting off power and water supplies. Supplies were left outside the homes rather than delivered directly, with residents saying Israeli forces blocked entry; the Israel Defense Forces disputed that account, stating that Qusra had been declared a closed military zone that barred Israeli civilians, but denied preventing aid transfers.

Separately on Friday, a group of settlers returned to erect a tent near the besieged properties — one day after an Israeli military operation dispersed them — before soldiers removed the structure. The IDF said it acted to protect local residents. The Qusra mayor told the BBC that Israeli forces were using some vacated Palestinian homes as barracks, a claim the military did not directly address.

The Israeli military had previously described the settlers' actions as 'deplorable' and pledged to investigate and arrest those responsible, and soldiers who were filmed praying with settlers face disciplinary proceedings. The episode has drawn renewed attention to the relative impunity of settler violence in the West Bank, where 127 Palestinian communities have experienced full or partial displacement since January 2023. Settlements are illegal under international law; the Israeli government has promoted their rapid expansion.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Announces Unprecedented Economic Isolation Plan for Iran as Blockade Declared 'Indefinite'
stories.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced this week that the United States will roll out sweeping new economic measures against Iran next week, describing them as "measures that have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country." The announcement coincides with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's declaration that the U.S. Navy can maintain its naval blockade of Iranian ports "indefinitely," rotating ships in and out as needed. Bloomberg reported Friday that the formal rollout of the plan is expected next week.

Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority pushed back on U.S. claims of controlling the Strait of Hormuz, posting on social media that "the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked and will not be reopened until Iran's conditions are accepted." Only a handful of ships have transited the strait this week despite Trump administration assertions of "full control." Ceasefire talks between the two countries remain in deadlock.

The intensifying economic pressure campaign comes amid growing concerns about the condition of U.S. forces deployed in the region. Military leaders have privately raised alarm inside the Pentagon and White House about morale and fatigue among the more than 50,000 troops deployed, particularly the roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been at sea for nearly seven months — well beyond a typical six-to-seven month deployment cycle.

The combination of an extended naval blockade and an unprecedented sanctions package represents a significant escalation in the U.S. effort to force Tehran's capitulation. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers, have warned that the prolonged deployment is unsustainable, while administration officials argue the pressure campaign is working and that the U.S. military has the capacity to maintain operations as long as necessary.

stories.headline: Trump Appeals to Supreme Court to Allow White House Ballroom Construction, Citing Security Needs
stories.summary:
President Trump filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court on Friday seeking permission to continue above-ground construction of a $400 million ballroom at the White House, after federal appeals court ruled last week that he lacked the unilateral authority to proceed without congressional approval. The DC Circuit Court of Appeals issued a 2-1 ruling on August 7 ordering a halt to above-ground construction, while permitting a sophisticated underground bunker beneath the ballroom to continue. The court gave Trump 14 days to appeal before its order took effect.

Solicitor General John Sauer argued in the Supreme Court filing that the East Wing construction is "absolutely required" for presidential security, citing past attempts on Trump's life. "The President of the United States of America is not a tenant, but rather the sole, elected head of the Executive Branch," Sauer wrote, calling the lower court's injunction "judicial overreach beyond the proper province of the federal courts."

The case was brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argued that Congress had not granted the executive branch "unfettered authority to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House." The appeals court agreed, stating that "whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide." The National Trust has until Tuesday noon to respond to Trump's petition.

The White House ballroom dispute is the first of Trump's major renovation or policy projects to reach the Supreme Court, and it comes amid a broader pattern of lower courts ruling against his administration across numerous legal fronts. The case raises significant questions about the scope of executive authority over federal property and the limits of presidential power absent explicit congressional authorization. New renderings released with the filing show stylistic changes including large gold presidential seals on the building's exterior.

stories.headline: Army Grounds All Apache Helicopter Training Missions After Fatal Texas Crash Kills Two Soldiers
stories.summary:
The U.S. Army announced Friday it is temporarily halting all Apache helicopter training missions nationwide following a fatal crash Wednesday near Salado, Texas, approximately 30 miles from Fort Hood. Chief Warrant Officer 2 Deontre T. Huey, 34, and Warrant Officer Seth L. Olmstead, 25, were killed when their helicopter went down in a grassy field. No cause has been released as the investigation is in its early stages.

A safety investigation team from the Army Combat Readiness Center in Fort Rucker, Alabama, is working to determine what caused the crash. "The stand-down will remain in effect until we have a better understanding of the root cause of the accident," the Army said in its statement. The Army stressed that combat Apache missions ongoing in the war with Iran — including operations around the Strait of Hormuz — are not affected by the stand-down.

The Army has taken similar action following past fatal crashes. Three years ago, the service grounded all aviation units after 12 soldiers died in separate crashes in Alaska and Kentucky. Aviation safety expert John Cox, CEO of Safety Operating Systems, called the move encouraging: "You're guessing until you get some hard answers," he said, adding that the stand-down signals the Army is making safety a priority.

The action comes against a backdrop of heightened scrutiny of Army aviation safety. The National Transportation Safety Board sharply criticized the Army's safety culture during its investigation of the January 2025 Black Hawk collision with an American Airlines jet near Washington, D.C., which killed 67 people. The NTSB found that the Army had poorly assessed safety risks in congested airspace before that crash.

stories.headline: France's Top Court Strikes Down Social Media Ban for Under-15s
stories.summary:
France's Constitutional Council struck down legislation Friday that would have banned children under 15 from creating social media accounts, ruling that the law constituted an infringement on freedom of expression that was neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate. The council also raised concerns about the law's age-verification requirements, finding they lacked adequate legal safeguards for privacy.

The legislation had been passed by French lawmakers in July and backed by President Emmanuel Macron, who had pledged to implement the ban in stages beginning in September, with full enforcement of existing accounts by January. France would have been the first European country to impose such a restriction. Following the ruling, Macron immediately directed Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to draft new legislation addressing the council's objections, with the president expressing determination to have a revised law in place by early 2027.

The ruling highlights the legal and technical difficulties governments face in restricting minors' access to social platforms. Opponents of the original law had questioned its viability, citing concerns about privacy, the reliability of age-verification tools, and the ease with which young people could circumvent such measures — as has been observed in Australia, which enacted a similar ban for under-16s in December.

The decision lands amid a broader wave of European efforts to limit children's social media use. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an EU-wide 'social media delay' for children in May, and the United Kingdom announced in June that under-16s would be banned from social media beginning in January 2027.

stories.headline: FDA Assigns Highest-Risk Class I Status to Recall of Nearly 1.6 Million Egg Cartons
stories.summary:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has elevated a recall of nearly 1.6 million cartons of eggs to Class I status, the agency's highest-risk designation, indicating a reasonable probability that the affected product could cause serious adverse health consequences or death. The recall affects eggs distributed across a wide geographic footprint and raises fresh public health concerns for consumers.

Class I recalls are reserved for the most serious violations of FDA standards, and the designation signals urgency for consumers to check whether they have affected products. The FDA separately noted that 14-ounce soup kits were distributed at Walmart stores in 29 states between June 30 and July 7 as part of a related food safety action.

The recall adds to ongoing food safety pressures affecting the egg supply, which has already been strained by elevated prices and supply disruptions. Consumers are advised to check product lot numbers against the recall notice and discard or return any affected cartons.

The FDA has not yet publicly detailed the specific contaminant or pathogen involved in the egg recall, but the Class I designation indicates the agency views the risk to public health as significant and immediate.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Attacks UAE Tankers in Strait of Hormuz; Regional Powers Condemn Strike
stories.summary:
Iran carried out what the United Arab Emirates and regional governments are calling "unprovoked attacks" on two tankers affiliated with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company as they transited the Strait of Hormuz on Friday. Qatar, Kuwait, Egypt and Bahrain all issued formal condemnations, with Qatar's Foreign Ministry calling the strike "a severe violation of international law, the freedom of maritime navigation, and a clear violation of UN Security Council resolution 2817." Bahrain called on the UN Security Council to take "firm and deterrent measures" to compel Iran to cease hostilities.

The attacks represent a significant escalation in the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, targeting vessels from a Gulf state that has not been a direct party to the war. The Strait of Hormuz remains a critical chokepoint for global energy supplies, and Iran has previously used access to it as leverage in negotiations.

Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the United States will unveil "unprecedented" economic isolation measures against Iran next week, intensifying pressure on Tehran to return to the negotiating table. Vice President Vance said Thursday that the administration's primary goal is keeping oil and gas prices stable for American consumers, and its second goal is ensuring Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon.

The Trump administration's stated war aims appear to be evolving. Vance conspicuously did not repeat earlier demands that the Strait be "open and toll-free," suggesting a possible shift in the terms Washington is seeking as negotiations remain stalled.

stories.headline: Update: Zambia Election Count Resumes After Violence Halts Tallying; Opposition Claims Victory
stories.summary:
Zambia's electoral commission resumed nationwide vote counting Friday evening after suspending the process earlier in the day over reports of attacks on polling staff, theft of marked ballot papers, and alleged military involvement at tallying centers. The commission said security forces had "contained" the threat and that new measures were in place to protect the integrity of the count. Results are expected by end of Sunday.

Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile expressed "grave concern" over the delays and said his party's own tabulation showed he had defeated incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, who is seeking a second five-year term. Mundubile called for the immediate publication of station-by-station results and investigations into alleged irregularities, including the movement of ballot boxes under suspicious circumstances.

Hichilema, who is credited with guiding Zambia through a difficult economic period but whose popularity has been dented by widespread public frustration over living standards, urged citizens to "remain peaceful, patient and patriotic" while awaiting official results. Polling day itself was largely peaceful, with high turnout reported across the country.

The election is being closely watched as a test of Zambia's standing as one of Africa's more stable democracies. The halt in counting and the opposition's fraud allegations have introduced uncertainty into what had appeared to be a competitive but orderly race.

stories.headline: Nigel Farage Wins Back Parliament Seat With 63% of Vote; Ethics Investigation Immediately Resumes
stories.summary:
Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party and a figure frequently cited as a potential future prime minister, reclaimed his Clacton parliamentary seat Friday after winning a special by-election with 63% of the vote. Farage had abruptly resigned his seat in July amid a parliamentary investigation into whether he failed to disclose a £5 million ($6.7 million) gift from an overseas cryptocurrency billionaire. He denied wrongdoing and called the election himself to seek a renewed mandate from voters.

The by-election drew a field of 34 candidates after Britain's major parties — Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats — boycotted the race, calling it a political stunt. The effective runner-up, with roughly 27% of the vote, was Count Binface, a satirical serial candidate who has previously challenged sitting prime ministers. Farage did not attend the official declaration ceremony, where he would have been required to stand alongside the other candidates.

Hours after the result was announced, the parliamentary watchdog that had suspended its ethics investigation when Farage stepped down confirmed it had resumed the probe. If investigators find he violated disclosure rules, Farage could face suspension from Parliament, potentially triggering yet another by-election in the same seat.

Farage hailed the result as an "overwhelming win" that increased his vote share compared to the last general election. Analysts cautioned, however, that drawing broad conclusions is difficult given the absence of genuine mainstream rivals and Farage's historically strong support in the conservative coastal constituency.

stories.headline: Consumer Sentiment Falls 8% in August as Retail Sales Slump, Raising Economic Concerns
stories.summary:
Two new economic data releases Friday painted a cautious picture of the U.S. consumer. The University of Michigan's preliminary consumer sentiment index fell to 51 in August from 55.2 in July, an 8% monthly decline that ended two consecutive months of improvement. Sentiment is now 12.4% below where it stood a year ago, though it remains above the spring lows when gasoline prices were at their peak.

Separately, the Census Bureau reported that retail sales slumped in July, suggesting consumers who had largely sustained economic growth through persistent inflation and high fuel costs may be pulling back. Economists said the weak retail figure, combined with a soft jobs report last week and subdued inflation readings earlier this week, gives the Federal Reserve room to hold off on any interest rate increases in the near term.

The decline in consumer sentiment was especially pronounced among Republican respondents, according to the University of Michigan data, a notable shift given that group had reported sharply improved confidence following the 2024 election. Analysts attributed the broader deterioration to ongoing anxiety about gasoline prices, tariff-driven cost increases, and uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict's effect on energy markets.

Taken together, the data suggest the economy may face a bumpier path in the second half of 2026, even as the underlying trend in consumer demand has not yet collapsed. Markets and Fed officials are likely to watch August and September data closely for signs of whether the July softness represents a temporary pause or the beginning of a more sustained slowdown.

stories.headline: WNBA Refuses to Rule Out Transgender Athletes as Two Former NBA Players Seek Entry Into League
stories.summary:
Two former NBA players who have declared themselves transgender have announced their intention to enter the WNBA draft, setting up a high-profile test of the league's policies on biological sex and athletic competition. WNBA presidents declined to rule out the possibility of biological males playing in the women's league, while also condemning what they characterized as bad-faith critics of the athletes involved.

The story is drawing significant national attention, with seven outlets spanning the political spectrum covering it. Supporters of transgender inclusion argue that blanket bans are discriminatory and that each athlete's eligibility should be evaluated individually. Critics, including many women's sports advocates and conservative commentators, contend that biological males retain physiological advantages that undermine competitive fairness in women's athletics.

The controversy arrives as transgender participation in sports remains one of the most divisive policy debates in American public life. The Trump administration has taken executive action to restrict transgender athletes in federally funded sports programs, and several states have enacted their own bans. The WNBA's response — or lack of a clear policy response — is likely to intensify pressure on the league from both directions.

The situation presents a broader cultural and legal flashpoint ahead of the 2026 midterms, with Republicans and some Democrats framing the issue as a matter of protecting women's competitive opportunities, while progressive and civil rights groups argue that transgender women are women and should be treated as such under league and federal anti-discrimination frameworks.

stories.headline: 'Unprecedented' Rain in Japan Kills Eight, Strands Thousands at Narita Airport
stories.summary:
Record rainfall described by Japanese authorities as 'unprecedented' struck eastern Japan on Thursday and Friday, killing at least eight people and cutting power to more than 20,000 households in Chiba prefecture. Chiba, which borders Tokyo, recorded more than 100 millimeters of rain per hour — roughly three times the August average and the highest single-hour precipitation volume ever recorded in Japan.

Local authorities issued their highest-level emergency alert, Level 5, on Thursday before downgrading it to Level 4 on Friday morning, while warning that landslide and flooding risks persist. More than 100,000 households were ordered to evacuate as rail services and major highways remained shut. Approximately 1,800 people spent the night sheltering in the Chiba Prefectural Government building, and around 1,800 passengers were stranded at Narita Airport overnight.

Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai called the event 'an extremely unusual situation, even by Japan's historical weather standards,' saying he had never encountered a comparable disaster in his career. The Japan Meteorological Agency attributed the deluge to warm, humid air colliding with cold air masses in highly unstable atmospheric conditions.

The storm is part of a broader pattern of extreme weather across East Asia this week. Japan, the Philippines, and China were struck by three simultaneous typhoons — Dolphin, Chan-Hom, and Peilou — in what meteorologists are forecasting to be an unusually active typhoon season. The Philippines has again shut schools and government offices across much of its northern regions due to ongoing flood threats.

stories.headline: White House Accuses More Than 40 Countries of Helping China Evade U.S. Tariffs
stories.summary:
The White House has released a report accusing China of routing tens of billions of dollars' worth of goods through more than 40 third-party countries to circumvent U.S. tariffs first imposed in 2018, costing the United States significant lost revenue annually. The report identifies transshipment — the practice of re-labeling or minimally processing Chinese goods in lower-tariff nations before exporting them to the United States — as the primary mechanism of evasion.

The administration contends the scheme has allowed Chinese exporters to undercut the intent of tariff policy designed to pressure Beijing on trade practices and protect American manufacturers. The report is expected to form the basis for potential new enforcement actions or secondary tariffs targeting countries identified as conduits.

The findings land at a sensitive moment in U.S. trade policy. Relations with China remain strained over a broad range of economic and security disputes, while some U.S. trading partners named in the report — including several in Southeast Asia — have been cultivating closer ties with Washington as an alternative to Chinese economic dependence. Critics of aggressive tariff enforcement warn that punishing allied or neutral nations could complicate diplomatic relationships and drive up consumer prices further.

Proponents of the crackdown, including domestic manufacturing groups, argue that closing transshipment loopholes is essential to making tariffs effective and preventing American industries from being undercut by artificially cheap Chinese goods arriving via third countries. The report is being watched closely by markets and trade attorneys as a signal of the administration's next moves on international commerce.

stories.headline: Instagram Accounts Fueling Dangerous Migrant Crossings Into Spanish Enclave of Ceuta
stories.summary:
A BBC investigation has found a network of interconnected Instagram profiles actively recruiting migrants from Morocco to attempt illegal crossings into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern tip of Africa, by portraying the dangerous route as safe and easy. The accounts, many of which offered paid advice for fees of up to 5,000 Moroccan dirhams (approximately £400), directed prospective migrants to use sewer pipes and other concealed routes to enter Ceuta.

The investigation follows a crisis last month in which roughly 78,000 migrants arrived in Ceuta by sea within hours, with at least 100 dying in the attempt according to the city's mayor. The accounts also spread misinformation about changes to Spanish immigration law and misrepresented Ceuta as a viable gateway to mainland Europe, when in reality it functions as a holding point with strict controls on onward travel.

Meta, which owns Instagram, told the BBC it has a team monitoring the Ceuta situation in real time and has been removing content that violates its policies. Several of the identified profiles were taken down after the BBC made contact with the company. However, new posts recommending another mass crossing attempt this weekend were still being actively promoted by Instagram's algorithm at the time of publication.

The crisis has inflamed tensions between EU member states that share open borders and drawn sharp criticism of the Spanish government's handling of border security. The revelation that commercial social media networks are being monetized to organize dangerous migration attempts adds a new dimension to the debate over platform accountability in migration and humanitarian contexts.

stories.headline: Update: Pentagon to Replace USS Abraham Lincoln as Troop Morale Concerns Mount; Military Pushes Back on False Reports
stories.summary:
The Pentagon plans to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln — one of two aircraft carriers deployed in the Middle East during the U.S.-Iran conflict — amid private concerns from military leaders about low morale and widespread fatigue among the more than 50,000 troops deployed in the region, according to three U.S. officials cited by NBC News. Some sailors and Marines have been at sea for more than nine months, well beyond the typical six-to-seven-month carrier deployment that includes regular port stops.

U.S. Central Command pushed back Thursday on a wave of recent media reports it called false, denying claims that seven sailors had died in a brawl aboard the Lincoln or that the ship had experienced a spike in suicidal ideation. 'These reports are FALSE,' CENTCOM said in a statement, noting the carrier has maintained an 84.4% crew reenlistment rate — among the highest of all aircraft carriers — and that no service members have died aboard the ship.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, speaking during a visit to Panama, said conditions on the Lincoln had been 'completely misrepresented' by media coverage, and praised the sailors for performing under 'austere conditions with less port calls.' The Pentagon's acknowledgment of fatigue and the planned carrier rotation, however, signals that the prolonged deployment is creating genuine operational strain, even as officials dispute the more extreme characterizations circulating online and in some news outlets.

The situation highlights a tension at the center of the ongoing Iran conflict: the military's need to sustain a demanding forward presence while managing the human costs of extended deployments. The planned rotation of the Lincoln would offer relief to its crew but also underscores the sustained tempo of U.S. operations in the region.

stories.headline: Taliban Detains Six Staff of Afghan Women's Rights Group; UN Employees Also Held
stories.summary:
Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have 'forcibly disappeared' six male staff members of the Women and Children Legal Research Foundation, a Kabul-based organization focused on women's and children's rights, Human Rights Watch reported Wednesday. The men were detained on July 18 after being summoned to their office to retrieve confiscated laptops and phones; their families have received no information about their whereabouts, condition, or any charges against them.

Separately, the United Nations disclosed that two Afghan employees of its political mission, UNAMA, were detained Sunday by Taliban intelligence in the western city of Herat. The U.N. said it has not been informed of the charges and has not been permitted to visit the detainees, and called on the Taliban to respect the privileges and immunities of U.N. officials.

The dual detentions come as the Taliban prepares to mark the fifth anniversary of its return to power on August 15, 2021, and as a deepening humanitarian crisis grips the country. The Taliban has systematically excluded women and girls from secondary education, higher education, employment, and most areas of public life since seizing power. 'The Taliban seems to consider any effort to assist women and girls a threat to their abusive rule,' said Macarena Sáez, women's rights director at Human Rights Watch, who called for the immediate release of the detained staff.

The incidents add to a pattern of Taliban crackdowns on civil society and international organizations. UNAMA said Thursday it had no information on whether the two separate detentions were connected. Human Rights Watch called on the Taliban to allow family members and lawyers to visit those held and to release them unless formally charged with a recognizable offense.

stories.headline: Vance Warns Republicans Not to Dismiss Young Voters' Economic Anxieties Fueling Interest in Socialism
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance issued a pointed warning to fellow Republicans on Thursday, urging the party not to simply dismiss or mock the growing interest in socialist ideas among younger Americans. Vance argued the GOP must directly address the underlying economic concerns — including surging housing costs and broad financial insecurity — that he said are driving young voters toward progressive politics.

'Our response to that can't just be to ignore the economic concerns that I think are feeding this rising interest in socialism,' Vance said, according to The Hill. The remarks reflect concern within some corners of the Republican Party that dismissing rather than engaging with the economic frustrations of younger voters could prove politically costly, particularly as progressive candidates have shown momentum in recent Democratic primaries.

The warning comes as Democrats are engaged in their own internal debate over the direction of the party. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings, speaking separately, described Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as the 'heir to the Sanders socialist movement' and the inspirational leader of an energized progressive wing. Some moderate Democrats have pushed back, arguing that a sharp leftward turn risks alienating swing voters ahead of the midterms.

The dueling conversations on both sides illustrate a broader realignment around economic populism, with both parties grappling with how to respond to voter anxiety over housing, wages, and the cost of living. Vance's remarks are notable in that they implicitly acknowledge economic grievances that some Republicans have been reluctant to validate.

stories.headline: ICE Agent Filmed Pointing Gun at Virginia Woman During Enforcement Stop
stories.summary:
A video showing a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pointing his firearm at a woman in Falls Church, Virginia, has circulated widely after the woman, Carolina Molina, shared it on Instagram, where it has been viewed by millions. Molina said she was out delivering business cards when ICE agents surrounded her car; she denied any threatening behavior toward officers.

The Department of Homeland Security offered a sharply different account, stating that Molina 'attempted to harm officers by weaponising her vehicle.' BBC Verify reviewed dashcam footage shared by Molina as part of its assessment of the competing claims. The incident has drawn significant public attention amid ongoing national debate over ICE enforcement tactics and the treatment of individuals during immigration operations.

The confrontation is one of several recent incidents involving ICE agents that have attracted public scrutiny and legal or congressional attention. Supporters of aggressive immigration enforcement argue agents must be prepared to protect themselves during unpredictable field operations. Critics contend that the footage exemplifies excessive use of force and intimidation against civilians who may not be enforcement targets.

The incident illustrates the volatile intersection of immigration enforcement, use-of-force policy, and public accountability at a moment when ICE operations have been significantly expanded and are the subject of intensified political debate.
